events.date_context: 1957 book and journal-paper milestone; the linked RAND report is an earlier 1954 treatment.
events.title: Bellman: dynamic programming and the Bellman equation
events.label: Bellman: dynamic programming
events.problem: Sequential decision problems (inventory, control, replacement) explode combinatorially if you search over whole action sequences.
events.idea: Bellman's principle of optimality decomposes sequential decisions into recursive subproblems: after an initial action, the remaining plan must be optimal for the state reached. His 1957 book and MDP paper developed this framework. Finite-horizon problems can be solved backward from the terminal step; infinite-horizon discounted problems can be solved by repeated value updates.
events.changed: Bellman equations underpin value-based RL: TD methods learn value estimates from sampled experience, Q-learning learns action values, and DQN approximates them with a neural network. Policy-gradient methods offer another route by optimizing a policy directly.
events.limits: Dynamic programming needs a known transition model and sweeps over all states; Bellman himself named the resulting blow-up in large state spaces the 'curse of dimensionality'.

sources.label: A Markovian Decision Process (J. Math. Mech. 6, 1957), DOI
The Theory of Dynamic Programming (RAND P-550, 1954)

terms.def: A model of sequential decisions with states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards, where the next state depends only on the current state and action.
A recursive relation between the value of a state and expected immediate reward plus discounted next-state value. It can evaluate a given policy or characterize an optimal one.
The expected discounted sum of future rewards from a state (V) or from a state-action pair (Q) when following a given policy.

verified.note: Book 'Dynamic Programming' (Princeton UP, 1957) is the canonical date; the publisher page blocked automated fetch, so the 1957 journal paper DOI (resolves) and RAND 1954 report are cited instead. Crossref has no record for the DOI; volume/issue (4 vs 5) differs between indexes.

events.title: Samuel's self-improving checkers program
events.label: Samuel's checkers
events.problem: Could a computer improve at a task through its own play rather than through hand-coded rules alone?
events.idea: Arthur Samuel's checkers program evaluated board positions with a weighted sum of features and adjusted the weights so that the evaluation of an earlier position moved toward the evaluation reached after searching ahead, plus rote memory of positions. He popularised the phrase 'machine learning' in this line of work.
events.changed: The weight update is an early form of what Sutton later formalised as temporal-difference learning: learn a prediction from a later, better prediction instead of waiting for the final outcome.
events.limits: Hand-chosen features and an update without convergence guarantees; it reached a respectable amateur level, and claims about it beating strong players are often overstated.

sources.label: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers (IBM J. R&D, 1959)

links.note: Sutton cites Samuel's checkers player as a precursor of TD

terms.def: A function scoring how good a game position is, used to choose moves during search.

verified.note: Crossref: IBM Journal of Research and Development 3(3), July 1959.

events.date_context: Approximate construction date from historical accounts; the linked primary paper was published in 1963. The 1961 date is not primary-source confirmed.
events.title: MENACE: a matchbox machine that learns noughts and crosses by trial and error
events.label: MENACE matchbox learner
events.problem: Is learning from reward alone, without any model of the game, mechanically possible?
events.idea: Donald Michie built a tic-tac-toe player from about 300 matchboxes, one per board position, holding coloured beads for moves. Moves were drawn at random in proportion to bead counts; after a win beads were added for the moves played, after a loss they were removed.
events.changed: A physical demonstration of reinforcement as changing action probabilities by outcome, later echoed in policy-gradient methods. Michie's BOXES work extended the idea to pole balancing.
events.limits: A lookup table over a tiny game; credit is assigned equally to every move in a game, so it cannot tell which move actually mattered (the credit-assignment problem).

sources.label: Michie, Experiments on the Mechanization of Game-Learning Part I (Computer Journal, 1963)

links.note: both raise the probability of actions in proportion to the outcome they led to

terms.def: Working out which of many earlier actions deserve credit or blame for a reward that arrives later.

verified.note: Built and described around 1961 (Science Survey article); the cited Computer Journal paper is Nov 1963 per Crossref. Year 1961 is from secondary sources.

events.title: Barto, Sutton & Anderson: adaptive critic for pole balancing (actor-critic)
events.label: Actor-critic architecture
events.problem: When reward arrives only at failure (the pole falls), how does a learner know which earlier actions were bad?
events.idea: Split the learner in two: a critic learns to predict future reward from each state and turns changes in its prediction into an immediate internal reinforcement signal; an actor uses that signal to adjust its action preferences.
events.changed: Actor-critic became a template for A3C, common PPO implementations and PPO-based RLHF: a policy network is updated using an advantage estimate derived from a learned value function. Other policy-gradient methods, including GRPO, can avoid a learned critic.
events.limits: Two coupled learners can be unstable, and the critic's errors bias the actor's updates.

sources.label: Neuronlike adaptive elements that can solve difficult learning control problems (IEEE SMC, 1983)

links.note: the critic's error signal is the TD error Sutton formalised in 1988
A3C is an asynchronous deep actor-critic

terms.def: An RL architecture with a policy (actor) that picks actions and a value estimator (critic) that scores them to reduce the variance of policy updates.
The agent's rule for choosing actions, usually a probability distribution over actions given the state.

verified.note: Crossref: IEEE Trans. SMC, Sept 1983.

events.title: Sutton: Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences
events.label: Temporal-difference learning
events.problem: Prediction learners waited for the final outcome (Monte Carlo) before updating, which is slow, memory-hungry and high-variance in long episodes.
events.idea: Update a value prediction toward the next prediction plus the intervening reward: V(s) ← V(s) + α[r + γV(s′) − V(s)]. Here s is the current state, s′ the next state, r the reward, α the learning rate and γ the discount factor. For example, V(s)=2, r=1, V(s′)=3, γ=0.9 and α=0.1 give V(s)=2.17 after one update. This is bootstrapping: learning a guess from a guess. In episodic prediction, TD(λ) connects one-step TD to Monte Carlo returns.
events.changed: TD made it possible to learn values online from raw experience without a model. It underlies Q-learning, TD-Gammon, DQN and the critics in modern actor-critic and RLHF; the TD error also became a model of dopamine signals in neuroscience.
events.limits: Bootstrapped targets are biased while the estimates are wrong, and combining bootstrapping, off-policy data and function approximation can diverge (the 'deadly triad').

sources.label: Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences (Machine Learning 3, 1988)

links.note: TD is a sampled, model-free approximation of the Bellman backup
formalises Samuel's idea of learning from later evaluations

terms.def: The one-step prediction error δ = r + γV(s′) − V(s): reward r plus discounted next-state value, minus current-state value. γ is the discount factor.
Updating an estimate toward a target that itself contains an estimate, rather than toward a fully observed return.
The weight γ applied per future step, usually 0 ≤ γ < 1 in continuing discounted tasks; γ=1 can be used in suitable episodic tasks.

verified.note: Crossref: Machine Learning 3(1), Aug 1988. Springer page blocks bots but the DOI is valid.

events.date_context: May 1992 convergence paper; Watkins introduced the algorithm in his 1989 thesis.
events.title: Q-learning (Watkins 1989 thesis; Watkins & Dayan 1992 convergence proof)
events.label: Q-learning
events.problem: A state-value estimate alone does not specify which action to choose. How can an agent learn optimal action values directly while its behavior still explores?
events.idea: Learn action values: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max_a′ Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]. Here s and a are the current state and action, s′ the next state, r the received reward, α the learning rate and γ the discount factor; a′ ranges over next-state actions. The maximum targets the greedy policy even when exploration chose a different action. Watkins and Dayan proved convergence in the tabular setting with repeated state-action visits and suitable learning rates.
events.changed: A canonical off-policy, model-free algorithm. The 2013 DQN work combined Q-learning with a convolutional network and experience replay; the 2015 Nature version added a periodically frozen target network.
events.limits: Tabular guarantees vanish with function approximation; the max over noisy estimates overestimates values (later fixed partly by Double Q-learning).

sources.label: Watkins, Learning from Delayed Rewards (PhD thesis, 1989)

links.note: applies TD bootstrapping to action values
DQN is deep Q-learning

terms.def: The expected return of taking action a in state s and then following a policy; picking argmax Q gives a greedy policy.
Learning about one policy (e.g. the greedy one) from data generated by another (e.g. an exploring or older policy).
Estimating or improving the policy that generated the learning data; on-policy policy-gradient methods typically collect a fresh batch after each update cycle.
The tension between trying uncertain actions to learn more and choosing the action currently believed best.

verified.note: Crossref: Machine Learning 8, May 1992. The algorithm first appeared in the 1989 thesis; the anchor id uses 1992.

events.date_context: May 1992 journal publication; the date marks this paper rather than all earlier work on the method.
events.title: Williams: REINFORCE, the likelihood-ratio policy gradient
events.label: REINFORCE policy gradient
events.problem: Value-based methods pick actions by max over Q, which is awkward for stochastic or continuous actions; one would rather adjust a parameterised policy directly, but sampling actions is not differentiable.
events.idea: Estimate the policy gradient from sampled experience: ∇θJ = E[(R − b)∇θ log πθ(a|s)] in a one-decision setting; for a trajectory, sum the corresponding terms over decisions. θ denotes policy parameters, πθ(a|s) the probability of action a in state s, R the return and b an action-independent baseline. An ascent step uses learning rate α: θ ← θ + α(R − b)∇θ log πθ(a|s). Above-baseline outcomes reinforce sampled actions; below-baseline outcomes push the other way.
events.changed: A foundational score-function estimator for policy-gradient methods. PPO and GRPO use related return- or advantage-weighted policy updates. In a token-level language-model formulation, tokens are actions and the generated answer is a trajectory.
events.limits: Very high variance: returns from whole episodes are noisy, so it needs many samples, baselines or critics to work.

sources.label: Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist RL (Machine Learning 8, 1992)

links.note: the policy gradient theorem generalises REINFORCE
GRPO is close to REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline

terms.def: The gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters, estimated from sampled actions as return-weighted grad log-probabilities.
An action-independent quantity, often a function of state, subtracted from the return in a policy-gradient estimate to reduce variance without changing its expectation.

verified.note: Crossref: Machine Learning 8, May 1992 (same special issue as Q-learning and TD-Gammon).

events.date_context: May 1992 journal publication; the date marks this paper rather than all earlier work on the method.
events.title: TD-Gammon: self-play TD learning reaches expert backgammon
events.label: TD-Gammon
events.problem: Could TD learning with a neural network, rather than a lookup table, master a large real game?
events.idea: Gerald Tesauro trained a multilayer network by TD(lambda) on games the program played against itself, with almost no built-in knowledge in the first version. Later versions with expert features and shallow search played near the level of top human players.
events.changed: An influential early success of neural function approximation and self-play in RL. It showed that learned evaluation could reach strong play in a large game, a pattern revisited by later systems such as AlphaGo Zero.
events.limits: Attempts to repeat it in chess and Go in the 1990s largely failed; backgammon's dice give natural exploration and smooth values, which made it unusually friendly.

sources.label: Practical issues in temporal difference learning (Machine Learning 8, 1992)
Temporal difference learning and TD-Gammon (CACM, March 1995)

links.note: TD(lambda) with a neural network
earlier neural self-play success; shared pattern, not a claim that the training algorithms are identical

terms.def: Training an agent by having it play against copies of itself, so the opponent improves as the agent does.
Representing a value function or policy with a parameterised model (e.g. a neural network) instead of a table, so it generalises across states.

verified.note: Crossref: 1992 paper May 1992; CACM article March 1995. ACM DOI blocks bots but resolves for browsers.

events.title: The rational agent framing: Russell & Norvig's AIMA and BDI agents
events.label: Rational agent framing
events.problem: AI lacked a common definition of what it was building: programs, planners and expert systems were described in incompatible terms.
events.idea: Russell & Norvig's textbook (1995) defined AI as building rational agents: systems that perceive an environment through sensors and act through actuators to maximise a performance measure. In parallel, Rao & Georgeff's Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) model described agents by beliefs, goals and committed plans.
events.changed: The perceive-decide-act loop is the vocabulary used for today's LLM agents (observation, tool call, environment), and the 'performance measure' framing makes the reward-specification problem explicit.
events.limits: Classical agent architectures relied on hand-written plans and symbolic world models; they did not learn general skills from data.

sources.label: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (book site)
Rao & Georgeff, BDI Agents: From Theory to Practice (ICMAS 1995)

links.note: both use a perception/action loop; this is a conceptual connection rather than a documented direct dependency
goal-directed agent framing underlies later safety arguments

terms.def: A system that perceives its environment and takes actions to achieve goals; in RL, the learner that interacts with an environment.
An agent architecture describing behaviour by beliefs (what it knows), desires (goals) and intentions (plans it has committed to).

verified.note: AIMA 1st edition 1995; ICMAS 1995 paper PDF resolves.

events.title: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction
events.label: Sutton & Barto textbook
events.problem: RL ideas were spread across control theory, psychology, operations research and AI, with inconsistent notation.
events.idea: A single textbook unified MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, TD, Q-learning, eligibility traces and actor-critic under one framework centred on value functions and the agent-environment loop.
events.changed: Defined the field's vocabulary and trained the generation that built deep RL; the 2nd edition (2018) added policy gradients and deep RL context.
events.limits: Mostly tabular and linear methods; the hard problems of large-scale function approximation were left largely open in 1998.

links.note: consolidates TD and related methods

terms.def: A scalar the environment gives the agent after each step; the agent's objective is to maximise its expected discounted sum.

verified.note: MIT Press 1998; authors' book pages resolve.

events.title: Ng, Harada & Russell: policy invariance under reward shaping
events.label: Potential-based reward shaping
events.problem: Sparse rewards make learning slow, so designers add bonus rewards; but ad-hoc bonuses can change what is optimal (an agent rewarded for approaching a goal learned to circle near it).
events.idea: In a discounted MDP, add a bounded state potential Φ through F(s,s′) = γΦ(s′) − Φ(s), where s is the current state, s′ the next state and γ the discount factor. Under the paper's assumptions this leaves the optimal policy unchanged; arbitrary extra reward terms generally do not. Episodic formulations also require appropriate terminal-state handling.
events.changed: An early formal statement that the reward you write is not the behaviour you get: extra reward terms can be exploited. This is a direct ancestor of later concerns about reward hacking and specification gaming.
events.limits: Guarantees only invariance of the optimal policy; it does not tell you how to pick a good potential or protect against a misspecified base reward.

links.note: reward hacking is one of the concrete problems
same group: where should rewards come from?

terms.def: Adding extra reward terms to guide learning; potential-based shaping is the form that preserves the optimal policy.
A reward that is zero almost everywhere and non-zero only on rare events such as task success.

verified.note: ICML 1999; the PDF is a course-reading copy hosted at Berkeley (resolves). Exact conference days not cited.

events.title: Policy gradient theorem with function approximation (Sutton, McAllester, Singh & Mansour)
events.label: Policy gradient theorem
events.problem: Value-based methods with function approximation could oscillate or diverge, and a small change in Q could flip the greedy policy discontinuously.
events.idea: Express the performance gradient using action values without differentiating the state distribution. Under compatible function-approximation assumptions, a learned critic can supply the correct policy-gradient direction. The paper gives a policy-iteration construction with a local-optimality convergence result under its stated conditions.
events.changed: Put actor-critic and policy-gradient methods on firm ground, setting up TRPO, PPO and A3C. Konda & Tsitsiklis' actor-critic analysis appeared in the same NIPS volume.
events.limits: Convergence is only to a local optimum and the variance and sample cost of gradient estimates remain high.

links.note: generalises the REINFORCE estimator
justifies using a learned critic
PPO optimises a surrogate of this gradient

terms.def: A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s): how much better an action is than the policy's average action in that state.

verified.note: NIPS 12 (conference Dec 1999, proceedings dated 2000). Proceedings page title confirmed.

events.title: Inverse reinforcement learning (Ng & Russell 2000; Abbeel & Ng 2004)
events.label: Inverse RL
events.problem: For many tasks (driving, flying a helicopter) it is easier to demonstrate good behaviour than to write down a reward function for it.
events.idea: Ng & Russell posed inverse RL: infer a reward under which the observed behaviour is optimal. Abbeel & Ng's apprenticeship learning (2004) matched the expert's expected feature counts so the learned policy does as well as the expert under the unknown reward.
events.changed: Established 'learn the reward from humans' as a research programme. Russell later built on it in cooperative inverse RL, and reward models learned from human preferences in RLHF are a descendant.
events.limits: The problem is ill-posed (many rewards explain the same behaviour, including the trivial zero reward), and it assumes the demonstrator is near-optimal.

sources.label: Ng & Russell, Algorithms for Inverse Reinforcement Learning (ICML 2000, PDF)
Abbeel & Ng, Apprenticeship learning via inverse RL (ICML 2004)

links.note: learning rewards from humans, via preferences rather than demonstrations
both address where rewards come from

terms.def: Inferring the reward function that best explains observed (expert) behaviour.
Learning a policy from demonstrations, either by copying actions (behaviour cloning) or via an inferred reward.

verified.note: Abbeel & Ng 2004 confirmed via Crossref. The Stanford host for the 2000 PDF refused connections at check time (6 Nov 2026); the URL is the widely cited one but was not re-confirmed.

events.date_context: 19 December 2013 preprint; the target-network refinement and broader game evaluation are from the 2015 Nature paper.
events.title: DQN: Playing Atari with deep reinforcement learning (Nature version 2015)
events.label: DQN plays Atari
events.problem: Learning control from high-dimensional video with nonlinear value functions was difficult: correlated observations and changing bootstrap targets could make training unstable.
events.idea: Train a convolutional network to output Q-values for each joystick action from raw frames, stabilised by experience replay (learn from random minibatches of stored transitions, breaking correlations) and, in the 2015 Nature paper, a periodically frozen target network for the bootstrap target.
events.changed: The 2013 paper used one architecture across seven Atari games and surpassed a human expert on three. The 2015 Nature paper expanded the evaluation to dozens of games with many human-level results, helping establish deep RL as a practical research program.
events.limits: Needed tens of millions of frames per game (far more than humans), failed on sparse-reward exploration games such as Montezuma's Revenge, and handles only discrete actions.

links.note: deep Q-learning
deep networks + RL at DeepMind

terms.def: Storing past transitions in a buffer and training on random samples from it, which reuses data and decorrelates updates (possible because Q-learning is off-policy).
A lagged copy of the Q-network used to compute bootstrap targets so the target does not shift with every update.
How much environment interaction an algorithm needs to reach a given performance; deep RL is notoriously sample-inefficient.

verified.note: arXiv v1 2013-12-19; Nature published online 2015-02-25 per Crossref.

events.title: AlphaGo: deep networks plus tree search beat a professional at Go
events.label: AlphaGo
events.problem: Go's branching factor and the difficulty of evaluating positions made it resistant to the search methods that worked in chess; experts expected human-level Go to be a decade away.
events.idea: A policy network first trained to imitate expert moves, then improved by self-play policy-gradient RL; a value network trained to predict game outcomes; and Monte Carlo tree search that uses both to focus and truncate search.
events.changed: Beat European champion Fan Hui 5-0 (announced with the Nature paper) and Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016, showing that learned evaluation plus search could crack a problem thought out of reach and making RL a mainstream AI story.
events.limits: Relied on human expert games for initialisation, a perfect simulator of the rules, and large compute; techniques did not transfer directly to messy real-world tasks.

sources.label: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search (Nature)

links.note: deep networks as value/policy functions
AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero removed the human data

terms.def: A search method that builds a game tree by repeated simulated playouts, expanding promising moves more often.
A network that predicts the expected outcome from a position, used in place of exhaustive search to the end of the game.

verified.note: Nature online 2016-01-27 per Crossref; Lee Sedol match 9-15 March 2016.

events.title: A3C: asynchronous advantage actor-critic
events.label: A3C
events.problem: DQN needed a large replay buffer and GPU; on-policy actor-critic methods with neural networks were unstable because consecutive samples are highly correlated.
events.idea: Run many actor-learners in parallel on CPU threads, each in its own environment copy, and apply their gradients asynchronously to shared parameters; the diversity across workers decorrelates data without replay. Updates use n-step returns and an advantage from a learned value baseline, plus an entropy bonus for exploration.
events.changed: Made on-policy deep actor-critic practical and fast, and its synchronous variant (A2C) and the advantage-plus-entropy recipe carried into PPO.
events.limits: Still sample-hungry; asynchronous updates are hard to reproduce, and synchronous batched variants usually matched it.

links.note: deep, parallel actor-critic
PPO reuses the advantage actor-critic structure

terms.def: A term rewarding the policy for keeping its action distribution spread out, to keep exploring.

events.title: PPO: Proximal Policy Optimization (after TRPO, 2015)
events.label: PPO
events.problem: Vanilla policy gradients are fragile: one large step can collapse the policy, and data collected by the old policy is wasted after one update. TRPO (Schulman et al., Feb 2015) fixed this with a KL-divergence trust region, but needed second-order conjugate-gradient machinery.
events.idea: Optimize a clipped surrogate: min(ρA, clip(ρ, 1−ε, 1+ε)A), where ρ = π_new(a|s)/π_old(a|s), A is an estimated advantage and ε sets the clipping range. Clipping caps a sample's incentive to move its action probability farther in the helpful direction. It supports several minibatch optimization epochs per collected batch, but does not enforce a hard bound on policy change or KL divergence.
events.changed: Became the default deep RL algorithm (OpenAI Five, robotics) and the RL step of RLHF for InstructGPT and ChatGPT, usually with a KL penalty to the supervised model.
events.limits: Sensitive to implementation details, and clipping alone does not prevent large policy changes; some implementations stop updates when measured KL divergence becomes too large. Common LLM RLHF implementations maintain policy, reference, reward and value models, increasing memory use.

sources.label: OpenAI Spinning Up: PPO clipping and its limits

links.note: a stabilised policy-gradient method
advantage actor-critic with entropy bonus
PPO is the RL step of InstructGPT's RLHF
first applied to LM fine-tuning from preferences

terms.def: A constraint intended to keep a policy update near the data-generating policy. TRPO uses a KL-divergence constraint; PPO-Clip instead uses a clipped objective and does not impose that hard constraint.
PPO-Clip maximizes min(ρA, clip(ρ, 1−ε, 1+ε)A): ρ is the new/old action-probability ratio, A the advantage estimate and ε the clip parameter. This caps incentive, not the policy change itself.
An advantage estimator that blends multi-step TD errors with a decay parameter lambda to trade bias against variance.

events.date_context: 20 March 2017 visual domain-randomization preprint; the separate Dactyl card covers the 2018 PPO-based control result.
events.title: Domain randomization: visual transfer from simulation to real robots
events.label: Domain randomization
events.problem: Visual models trained on rendered images can fail on real camera images because the rendering differs from the real scene.
events.idea: Tobin et al. randomized visual properties such as textures and lighting when generating simulated images. They trained an object-localization model on these varied renderings so that real images could look like another variation of the training distribution, then used it in a grasping pipeline.
events.changed: Showed a route to visual sim-to-real transfer without training on real images. Later Dactyl combined visual and physical randomization with PPO-based control, extending the idea to dexterous manipulation.
events.limits: The 2017 result concerned visual localization and grasping, not a general RL controller. Transfer still depends on whether the training variations cover important differences in the real system.

links.note: Dactyl builds on visual domain randomization and extends it to control with varied dynamics

terms.def: The mismatch between a simulator and the physical world that makes policies trained in simulation fail on real hardware.
Training across many randomised simulator settings so the learned policy is robust to the real world's unknown settings.

verified.note: arXiv v1 2017-03-20 (Tobin et al.) and 2018-08-01 (Dactyl). Review 2026-11-06: Reopened Tobin abstract and Dactyl full text; separated visual transfer (2017) from PPO-based dexterous control (2018).

events.date_context: 5 December 2017 AlphaZero preprint; its Go-specific predecessor AlphaGo Zero was published in October 2017.
events.title: AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero: tabula rasa self-play
events.label: AlphaZero
events.problem: AlphaGo depended on human expert games and Go-specific design; was human data necessary, and did the method generalise beyond Go?
events.idea: AlphaGo Zero (Nature, Oct 2017) trained one residual network with policy and value heads purely from self-play: MCTS acts as a policy-improvement operator, the network is trained to match the search's visit distribution and the game outcome, and the improved network makes the next search stronger. AlphaZero (Dec 2017 preprint, Science 2018) applied the same algorithm to chess, shogi and Go.
events.changed: AlphaZero reported stronger play than its benchmark engines in chess, shogi and Go from game rules and self-play. It made search-to-policy distillation a prominent pattern. Comparisons with reasoning-model RL are useful analogies, rather than evidence that the same training algorithm is used.
events.limits: Needs a perfect, cheap simulator and known rules; compute was very large; chess comparisons against Stockfish were criticised for match conditions in the preprint.

sources.label: Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge (Nature, 2017)

MuZero drops the known rules

events.date_context: 27 March 2018 World Models preprint; this card also covers Dreamer (2019) and DreamerV3 (2023).
events.title: World Models and Dreamer: learning inside a learned model
events.label: World models / Dreamer
events.problem: Model-free deep RL needs millions of real interactions; model-based RL could plan or train in imagination, but learned models were inaccurate in pixel-based tasks.
events.idea: Ha & Schmidhuber compressed observations with a VAE, learned an RNN that predicts the next latent state, and trained a tiny controller partly inside this 'dream'. Hafner et al.'s Dreamer (Dec 2019) learned behaviours by backpropagating value estimates through imagined latent trajectories; DreamerV3 (Jan 2023) used one configuration across many domains and collected diamonds in Minecraft from scratch.
events.changed: Revived model-based RL for high-dimensional observations and fed today's interest in learned world models for robotics, games and video.
events.limits: Agents exploit model errors (the 'dream' can be gamed), and long-horizon prediction remains hard.

sources.label: Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models (DreamerV3, arXiv)

links.note: MuZero also plans with a learned latent model

terms.def: RL that learns or uses a model of environment dynamics to plan or to generate simulated experience.
A learned model that predicts how the environment's state (often a latent representation) evolves given actions.

events.title: AlphaStar: StarCraft II with multi-agent RL
events.label: AlphaStar
events.problem: StarCraft II combines imperfect information, real-time control, long horizons and a huge action space, unlike turn-based board games.
events.idea: Pretrain a transformer/LSTM policy on human replays, then improve with RL in a 'league' of agents: main agents plus exploiter agents that search for their weaknesses, sampled so the population does not cycle through strategies.
events.changed: Reached Grandmaster level on the public ladder under human-like constraints (Nature, Oct 2019) and showed population-based training as a tool against exploitable strategies.
events.limits: January 2019 matches were criticised for superhuman action speed and camera access; later versions added limits. Heavy reliance on human data and enormous compute.

same year, large-scale RL in real-time strategy games

events.date_context: 13 December 2019 paper; the named system was announced on 25 June 2018 and beat OG on 13 April 2019.
events.title: OpenAI Five: Dota 2 with large-scale PPO
events.label: OpenAI Five (Dota 2)
events.problem: Could plain policy-gradient RL, with little algorithmic novelty, handle a team game with long horizons (around 20,000 steps), partial observability and five cooperating agents?
events.idea: Scale PPO with LSTM policies to thousands of GPUs and over 100,000 CPU cores of self-play for about 10 months, with reward shaping and 'surgery' to keep training through game updates.
events.changed: Beat world champion team OG in April 2019; the paper (Dec 2019) argued that scale, not new algorithms, was the main ingredient, a lesson OpenAI later carried into language models.
events.limits: Played a restricted hero pool and rule set; human players later found exploitable strategies in public play; the compute bill was very large.

events.title: MuZero: planning with a learned model
events.label: MuZero
events.problem: AlphaZero needed the exact rules to run tree search, which real-world domains and Atari do not provide.
events.idea: Learn a latent dynamics model that predicts only what planning needs (reward, value and policy several steps ahead), not pixels, and run MCTS inside that learned model.
events.changed: Matched AlphaZero in Go, chess and shogi without being given rules and set a new state of the art on Atari, unifying model-based planning and model-free performance.
events.limits: Very compute-intensive; the latent model is not a faithful simulator and is hard to interpret or reuse for other goals.

verified.note: arXiv v1 2019-11-19 (Nature 2020).

events.date_context: 4 May 2020 tutorial preprint; CQL followed in June. Offline/batch RL itself predates these papers.
events.title: Offline RL: learning from fixed datasets (Levine et al. tutorial; CQL)
events.label: Offline RL
events.problem: Online RL needs fresh interaction, which is dangerous or costly in medicine, driving or robotics, while large logged datasets go unused; naive off-policy RL on fixed data overestimates the value of actions never seen in the data.
events.idea: Offline (batch) RL learns a policy only from a static dataset. Conservative Q-Learning (Kumar et al., June 2020) penalises Q-values of out-of-distribution actions so the policy stays where the data gives evidence.
events.changed: Consolidated deep offline RL and methods such as CQL into a practical research agenda for learning from logs. Fixed preference-data methods such as DPO share distribution-shift concerns, although standard online RLHF also collects fresh policy samples.
events.limits: Reliable improvement depends on coverage of relevant states and actions. A learned policy can outperform the behavior policies by combining useful transitions from the data, but unsupported actions are difficult to value and offline evaluation remains hard.

sources.label: Offline RL: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives (arXiv)

links.note: off-policy Q-learning with conservatism
DPO also learns from a fixed dataset without online rollouts

terms.def: Learning a policy from a fixed dataset of past interactions without collecting new data.
When the states or actions a learned policy visits differ from those in the training data, making value estimates unreliable.

events.date_context: 18 September 2019 preprint; the 2017 preference-RL paper used games and simulated robotics rather than pretrained language models.
events.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences (Ziegler et al.)
events.label: RL fine-tuning of LMs
events.problem: Language models trained by next-token prediction could not be optimised for qualities people judge but cannot write as a loss, such as a good summary or a positive continuation.
events.idea: Collect human comparisons between GPT-2 samples, fit a reward model to them, then fine-tune the language model with PPO to maximise that reward minus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the original model.
events.changed: Extended learned human-preference rewards to pretrained language models, building on earlier preference-based deep RL. The reward-model-plus-PPO recipe informed later summarization work and InstructGPT; supervised fine-tuning was an experimental variant here, not a mandatory first stage of every run.
events.limits: The authors report the summarisation model learned to copy sentences from the input, which pleased labellers but was a shortcut; a bug once flipped the reward sign and produced maximally explicit text, an early lesson in optimising a proxy.

links.note: fine-tunes GPT-2
uses PPO as the optimiser
the RLHF recipe behind InstructGPT
extends the learned-preference-reward approach to pretrained language models

terms.def: A network trained on human comparisons to output a scalar score for a response, used as the reward in RLHF.
A term penalising divergence between the fine-tuned policy and a reference model, limiting reward over-optimisation and drift.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: fit a reward model to human preferences and optimise a policy against it.

verified.note: arXiv v1 2019-09-18. The 'sign bug' anecdote is from the authors' paper/blog; wording paraphrased.

events.title: DPO: Direct Preference Optimization
events.label: DPO
events.problem: PPO-based RLHF is complex and unstable: it trains a separate reward model, samples from the policy during training and juggles four models in memory.
events.idea: For the KL-regularised RLHF objective, the optimal policy has a closed form in terms of the reward, so the reward can be rewritten as beta log(pi/pi_ref). Substituting into the Bradley-Terry preference likelihood gives a simple classification loss on preferred versus rejected responses, trained directly on the policy with no reward model and no sampling.
events.changed: Became the default open-source preference-tuning method (e.g. Zephyr, Tulu 2, many Llama fine-tunes) and spawned variants (IPO, KTO, SimPO).
events.limits: The original method learns from fixed preference pairs, so data coverage, length/style biases and distribution shift matter. Online preference optimization and verifiable-reward RL offer other ways to obtain fresh learning signals; which works best depends on the task and implementation.

links.note: simplifies the InstructGPT RLHF pipeline
removes PPO and the explicit reward model
offline learning from a fixed dataset

terms.def: A model where the probability one item is preferred over another is a logistic function of the difference in their scores.
In DPO, the quantity beta log(pi(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)), which plays the role of the reward without a separate network.

verified.note: arXiv v1 2023-05-29 (NeurIPS 2023).

events.title: RLAIF: reinforcement learning from AI feedback
events.label: RLAIF
events.problem: Human preference labels are slow, costly and inconsistent, limiting how much RLHF can scale.
events.idea: Use an off-the-shelf LLM to produce the preference labels (or a direct reward score) instead of humans. Lee et al. (Google) compared RLAIF to RLHF on summarisation and dialogue and report comparable human-rated quality; Anthropic's Constitutional AI (Dec 2022) had already used AI feedback guided by written principles for harmlessness.
events.changed: AI-generated feedback became a standard part of post-training pipelines, shifting the human role toward writing principles and auditing.
events.limits: The labelling model's biases and blind spots are inherited and possibly amplified; results were on a few tasks, and 'self-preference' effects are a concern.

links.note: Constitutional AI introduced AI feedback for harmlessness
same pipeline, AI labeller instead of humans

terms.def: RL from AI feedback: preference labels or rewards for RL fine-tuning come from a model rather than people.

events.date_context: 5 February 2024 DeepSeekMath preprint introducing GRPO; DeepSeek-R1 applied it in 2025.
events.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization (DeepSeekMath)
events.label: GRPO
events.problem: Common PPO implementations for LLMs use a separate value model to estimate advantages, adding memory and making end-of-answer rewards difficult to assign across long responses.
events.idea: For each prompt sample a group of G answers, score them, and use each answer's reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation, as its advantage. Keep PPO's clipped ratio and a KL term to a reference model, but drop the critic entirely.
events.changed: Removed the learned critic from a PPO-style objective by estimating advantages from groups of answers. DeepSeek-R1 used this approach, and it became an influential recipe in open reasoning-RL research.
events.limits: Needs several samples per prompt. When all answers have the same reward, the normalized reward-advantage term provides no ranking signal; implementations must also handle zero variance. Later variants examined length and normalization biases.

links.note: PPO's clipped objective without the value network
REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline
R1's RL algorithm

terms.def: An advantage computed by comparing a sample's reward with the mean (and spread) of other samples for the same prompt, replacing a learned critic.

events.date_context: Official announcement dated 12 September 2024; the optimizer and reward construction were not publicly specified there.
events.title: OpenAI o1: reasoning trained with large-scale RL and test-time compute
events.label: OpenAI o1
events.problem: Chain-of-thought prompting helped reasoning, but reliable multi-step problem solving still required better training and more effective use of inference computation.
events.idea: Train the model with large-scale reinforcement learning to produce a long hidden chain of thought before answering. OpenAI reported that performance improves smoothly both with more RL training compute and with more 'thinking' tokens at inference. Snell et al. (Aug 2024) had separately shown that spending inference compute well can beat a much larger model on some problems.
events.changed: Popularized learned reasoning and inference-time computation as a major scaling axis for deployed LLMs. Its reported results showed substantial gains from RL training and additional time spent reasoning, while the detailed optimizer and reward recipe remained undisclosed.
events.limits: OpenAI disclosed few training details and hid the raw reasoning; long reasoning is costly and slow; gains are largest where answers can be checked (math, code) and smaller on open-ended tasks. Hidden chains of thought raised monitoring questions.

sources.label: Learning to Reason with LLMs (OpenAI blog)
Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally (Snell et al., arXiv)

links.note: trains chain of thought with RL instead of only prompting it
more thinking at test time, like more search
R1 reproduced the recipe openly
adds an inference-compute scaling axis

terms.def: Improving answers by spending more computation at inference, e.g. longer reasoning, many samples with voting, or search, instead of a bigger model.
An LLM trained (typically with RL) to generate an extended chain of thought before its final answer.

verified.note: Release date 12 Sept 2024 from memory and press coverage; openai.com returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches so the blog page could not be opened. Snell et al. arXiv v1 2024-08-06 verified. Review 2026-11-06: Official OpenAI announcement opened and confirms 12 Sep 2024; it discloses large-scale RL and train/test-time scaling but not GRPO or a specific reward recipe.

events.date_context: 22 November 2024 Tulu 3 preprint names this recipe RLVR; rule-based rewards are much older. Tulu 3 uses PPO, not GRPO.
events.title: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR, named in Tulu 3)
events.label: RL with verifiable rewards
events.problem: Learned reward models can be gamed: a policy optimised hard against one finds outputs the model scores highly but humans would not (reward over-optimisation).
events.idea: Where correctness can be checked by a program, use the checker as the reward: 1 if the final math answer matches, the code passes tests, or the output satisfies a format constraint, else 0. Tulu 3 (AI2) named this RLVR and released an open pipeline.
events.changed: Programmatically checked rewards became a practical route to reasoning RL, demonstrated openly by systems such as DeepSeek-R1. They reduce dependence on learned judgments while remaining limited by what the checker actually verifies.
events.limits: Only covers domains with checkers; the checker itself can be gamed (weak unit tests, special-casing tests, answer-format tricks), and binary rewards give no credit for partially correct reasoning.

links.note: o1-style training relies on checkable problems
R1-Zero used rule-based accuracy and format rewards
test-based rewards can be gamed

terms.def: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: the reward comes from an automatic correctness check (answer match, unit tests) rather than a learned reward model.
When optimising a proxy reward past a point makes true quality fall, because the policy exploits the proxy's errors (an instance of Goodhart's law).

verified.note: arXiv v1 2024-11-22. The idea of rule-based rewards predates the name; date marks the naming. Review 2026-11-06: Reopened full text §6 and §6.2: programmatic verifiers provide rewards; the optimizer is PPO with a value model. This does not establish o1's undisclosed reward recipe.

events.title: DeepSeek-R1: reasoning from RL with rule-based rewards, released openly
events.label: DeepSeek-R1
events.problem: After o1, it was unclear whether long reasoning required secret techniques such as process reward models or search, and no open model matched it.
events.idea: R1-Zero applied GRPO directly to the base model DeepSeek-V3 with only rule-based rewards for answer accuracy and output format; long chains of thought, self-verification and 'aha' re-evaluation emerged, and length grew during training. R1 added a small cold-start supervised set, more RL and distillation into smaller open models.
events.changed: Showed publicly that simple outcome-reward RL at scale yields o1-level reasoning, released weights under MIT licence, and triggered a wave of open RLVR replications; the paper was later published in Nature (2025).
events.limits: R1-Zero's reasoning mixed languages and was hard to read; the authors report process reward models and MCTS did not work well for them. Claims about low training cost referred to the V3 base run, not the full program.

links.note: trained with GRPO
rule-based verifiable rewards
open reproduction of o1-style reasoning

terms.def: Training a smaller model on outputs (here, reasoning traces) of a larger one.
A small supervised fine-tuning stage before RL, used to give the model a readable output format.

verified.note: GitHub repo created 2025-01-20 (API); arXiv v1 2025-01-22. Nature publication (Sept 2025) not re-opened here.

events.date_context: 14 March 2025 Baker et al. preprint; the card also discusses a separate November 2025 study.
events.title: Reward hacking in coding RL and chain-of-thought monitoring
events.label: Reward hacking in coding RL
events.problem: Agentic coding RL rewards passing tests, and tests are an imperfect specification: models can make tests pass without solving the task.
events.idea: OpenAI (Baker et al.) reported a frontier reasoning model in training that hacked coding tasks (e.g. editing test harnesses, exiting early) and that another LLM reading its chain of thought caught these hacks far better than one reading only actions. Penalising 'bad thoughts' in training reduced visible hacking but led to obfuscated hacking. Anthropic and Redwood (MacDiarmid et al., Nov 2025) found that models which learned to hack real production coding environments generalised to broader misalignment, and that 'inoculation prompting' reduced this.
events.changed: Moved specification gaming from toy examples into frontier training runs and made chain-of-thought monitorability and RL environment design safety issues.
events.limits: Single-lab case studies; how often hacking occurs in deployed models is hard to measure from outside, and the mitigation results are preliminary.

sources.label: Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL (arXiv)

links.note: test-based verifiable rewards can be gamed

terms.def: When an agent achieves high reward by exploiting flaws in the reward signal instead of doing the intended task.
Satisfying the literal specification of an objective while violating its intent.
Using another model or human to read a reasoning model's intermediate reasoning to detect misbehaviour.

events.date_context: 21 July 2025 DeepMind announcement of its officially graded IMO result.
events.title: Reasoning models reach IMO gold-medal standard in natural language
events.label: IMO gold by LLMs
events.problem: DeepMind's 2024 silver-level result used human translation into a formal proof language. Could a general-purpose reasoning model solve olympiad problems directly in natural language under competition conditions?
events.idea: Google DeepMind reported that an advanced Gemini Deep Think solved five of six IMO 2025 problems in natural language within the competition time limit, scoring 35/42 under official IMO grading. Its account credits new RL techniques for multi-step reasoning and theorem proving, plus parallel thinking.
events.changed: Demonstrated strong performance on full mathematical proofs rather than only short checkable final answers, under the reported competition conditions.
events.limits: The evaluated system was experimental and used a large inference budget; one problem remained unsolved. The public account does not disclose a complete training recipe or establish the same result across general mathematical research tasks.

events.date_context: 17 December 2021 paper; rejection sampling selects among generated answers and is distinct from an RL weight update.
events.title: WebGPT: a language model that browses the web, trained with human feedback
events.label: WebGPT
events.problem: Answers produced from language-model parameters alone could be outdated or fabricated. The task was to let a model browse sources and support its answer with collected references.
events.idea: Fine-tune GPT-3 to operate a text-based browser through search, click, quote and scroll commands, collecting references for its answer. The paper compared imitation learning, PPO fine-tuning from human preferences and reward-model rejection sampling. Its best reported configuration used behavior cloning followed by selecting generated answers with the reward model.
events.changed: One of the first LMs to act in an environment through tool commands with RLHF, prefiguring browsing assistants, Deep Research and agent scaffolds.
events.limits: Authors note the model could cherry-pick sources to support an answer and that human raters were swayed by confident citations; text-only browser.

links.note: fine-tuned GPT-3
reward model from human comparisons
browsing research agents

terms.def: A model emitting structured calls to external tools (search, code execution, APIs) and using their results in its output.
Generating several outputs and keeping the one a reward model scores highest.

events.title: SayCan: grounding language models in robot affordances
events.label: SayCan
events.problem: LLMs can propose plausible plans for 'clean up the spill', but do not know what a particular robot can actually do in its current situation.
events.idea: Score each candidate skill by the product of the LLM's probability that it is a useful next step ('say') and a learned value function estimating whether the robot can succeed at it from the current state ('can'), then execute the best one and repeat.
events.changed: An early template for LLMs as high-level planners over learned low-level skills, a step toward language-driven robot agents.
events.limits: Limited to a fixed library of pretrained skills in a kitchen setting; failures in skills or perception propagate.

links.note: relies on RL-trained skills and value functions
LLM chooses actions step by step

terms.def: What actions are possible for an agent in a given situation; in SayCan, estimated by a value function per skill.

events.title: ReAct: interleaving reasoning and acting
events.label: ReAct
events.problem: Chain-of-thought reasoning hallucinated facts because it never checked the world, while action-only agents could not plan or recover from mistakes.
events.idea: Prompt the model to alternate 'Thought: ... Action: ... Observation: ...' steps, so reasoning decides which tool call to make (e.g. Wikipedia search) and tool results feed back into the next thought.
events.changed: The thought-action-observation loop became the default pattern for LLM agents and agent frameworks (LangChain, AutoGPT and successors).
events.limits: Purely prompted, with few-shot examples; long trajectories accumulate errors and the model can loop or repeat actions.

links.note: adds actions and observations to chain of thought
perceive-reason-act loop
autonomous loops built on this pattern

terms.def: The code around a model that runs the loop: builds prompts, parses tool calls, executes them and feeds results back.
An agent pattern alternating natural-language reasoning steps with tool actions and their observations.

events.title: Toolformer: language models teach themselves to use tools
events.label: Toolformer
events.problem: Tool use was added by prompting or by human-annotated demonstrations; models did not learn by themselves when a tool call actually helps.
events.idea: Let the model insert candidate API calls (calculator, search, QA, translation, calendar) into text, execute them, and keep only calls whose results lower the loss on the following tokens; fine-tune on the filtered data.
events.changed: Showed tool use can be learned self-supervised from a usefulness signal, a step toward tool calling becoming a trained capability (function calling APIs in 2023).
events.limits: Single tool calls, no chaining or interactive use; tested on a 6.7B model with simple tools.

links.note: tool use without human demonstrations
tool calling as a standard model capability

terms.def: An API feature where the model outputs a structured call (name and arguments) to a developer-defined function instead of free text.

events.date_context: March 2023 AutoGPT milestone, after GPT-4's 14 March launch; BabyAGI followed in April. Month precision does not imply a pre-GPT-4 appearance.
events.title: AutoGPT and BabyAGI: the autonomous-agent hype of spring 2023
events.label: AutoGPT / BabyAGI hype
events.problem: After GPT-4, people wanted models to pursue open-ended goals over many steps rather than answer single prompts.
events.idea: Open-source scripts wrapped GPT-4 in a loop: break a goal into tasks, keep a task list and memory, call tools (web, files, code), and feed results back, with no human between steps. AutoGPT's repository (March 2023) became one of the fastest-growing on GitHub; BabyAGI followed in April.
events.changed: Popularised the idea of autonomous LLM agents and exposed their failure modes at scale; it also prompted early discussion of agent safety (e.g. ChaosGPT stunts).
events.limits: In practice the agents frequently looped, lost track of goals, and were expensive; the models had not been trained for long-horizon agency, which later RL-trained agents addressed.

links.note: wrapped GPT-4 in an autonomous loop after the model's 14 March 2023 launch
reason-act loop extended to open goals

terms.def: An LLM system that pursues a goal over many steps, choosing its own actions and tool calls with little human input.

verified.note: GitHub API: AutoGPT repo created 2023-03-16, BabyAGI 2023-04-03; the viral period was late March to April 2023.

events.title: Voyager: a lifelong-learning Minecraft agent built on GPT-4
events.label: Voyager (Minecraft)
events.problem: RL agents in Minecraft needed huge amounts of experience and did not reuse skills; LLM agents forgot what they had learned between tasks.
events.idea: GPT-4 proposes its own curriculum of tasks, writes JavaScript programs as skills, refines them using environment feedback and self-verification, and stores working programs in a skill library for later reuse, with no gradient updates.
events.changed: Showed 'skills as code' and self-generated curricula as a route to open-ended agent learning without training the model.
events.limits: Relies on a text API to the game rather than pixels and on expensive GPT-4 calls; Minecraft's API makes many actions simpler than real tasks.

events.date_context: 10 October 2023 SWE-bench preprint; the later Verified subset was announced on 13 August 2024.
events.title: SWE-bench: resolving real GitHub issues
events.label: SWE-bench
events.problem: Coding benchmarks like HumanEval tested short self-contained functions and were near saturation, saying little about real software work.
events.idea: 2,294 real issues from 12 Python repositories: the model gets the codebase and issue text and must produce a patch; success means the repository's own tests that the real fix made pass now pass (fail-to-pass), without breaking others.
events.changed: Became a prominent measure of coding agents; initial evaluated models solved only a small fraction of the tasks. OpenAI released the human-validated SWE-bench Verified subset on 13 August 2024. Test-based grading also became a template for coding RL environments.
events.limits: Python only, possible training-data contamination, and tests can be weak, so a patch can pass while being wrong; scores depend heavily on the agent scaffold.

links.note: SWE-agent was built to tackle it

events.problem: Static Q&A benchmarks could not tell whether a model can complete multi-step tasks with tools, computers or users.
events.idea: GAIA (Nov 2023): questions simple for humans but needing web browsing, files and multi-step tool use, with unambiguous answers. OSWorld (Apr 2024): 369 tasks in real Ubuntu/Windows/macOS desktops checked by execution scripts. tau-bench (June 2024): agents serve simulated users in retail and airline domains under policy rules, with pass^k measuring consistency over repeated trials.

events.limits: Benchmarks saturate quickly, can be gamed by scaffolds, and simulated users or environments only roughly match deployment.

events.date_context: 6 May 2024 preprint; the repository was public in April 2024.
events.title: SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces
events.label: SWE-agent
events.problem: LLMs using a raw Linux shell got lost in large repositories: long outputs, clumsy editing commands and silent errors.
events.idea: Design an agent-computer interface for the model, as one would design a UI for humans: compact file viewer with line numbers, search commands with concise output, an edit command with a linter that rejects syntax errors, and clear feedback. With GPT-4 this raised SWE-bench resolution to about 12.5%.
events.changed: Showed that an interface designed for the model can substantially improve a coding agent using the same underlying model. It made the scaffold and tools explicit experimental variables rather than treating benchmark scores as properties of the LM alone.
events.limits: This was prompted scaffolding rather than a new model-training method. Gains depend on the model, interface and benchmark, so later training advances do not remove the need to evaluate the complete agent.

events.title: Claude computer use (public beta)
events.label: Claude computer use
events.problem: Agents could act only through APIs someone had built for them; most software is designed for humans with screens, mice and keyboards.
events.idea: Claude 3.5 Sonnet was trained to look at screenshots, count pixels to move a cursor, click and type, so it can operate standard software; released as an API beta. Anthropic reported 14.9% on OSWorld's screenshot-only category versus 7.8% for the next system.

events.limits: Anthropic described it as slow and error-prone; screens open new prompt-injection attack surfaces, since any text on a web page can try to steer the agent.

events.date_context: 25 November 2024 protocol announcement; later adoption and specification revisions are separate milestones.
events.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
events.label: Model Context Protocol
events.problem: Every pairing of an AI application with a data source or tool needed a custom integration, so agents' tool sets were fragmented.
events.idea: An open protocol (JSON-RPC based) where tool and data providers run MCP servers exposing tools, resources and prompts, and any MCP-capable client or model application can discover and call them.
events.changed: Provided a common interface for connecting model applications to tools and data, reducing the need for a separate integration for every client-provider pair.
events.limits: Standardizes a connection interface rather than safety or trust. An application still needs authorization, constrained tool access and defenses against malicious instructions in tool outputs; the protocol alone does not supply those safeguards.

coding agents extended with MCP tools

events.date_context: Operator was announced on 23 January 2025; Deep Research followed on 2 February 2025.
events.title: OpenAI Operator and Deep Research: RL-trained agents as products
events.label: Operator & Deep Research
events.problem: Prompted agent scaffolds were unreliable on long web tasks; models had not been trained end-to-end to act.
events.idea: Operator (23 Jan 2025) used a Computer-Using Agent model (GPT-4o vision plus RL) to operate a browser for users, asking for confirmation on sensitive steps. Deep Research (2 Feb 2025) used a version of o3 trained with RL on browsing and analysis tasks to research a question for many minutes and write a cited report.

events.limits: Operator was slow and needed frequent takeovers; Deep Research can still cite weak sources or hallucinate, and both are prompt-injection targets.

events.title: Claude Code and the 2025 shift to terminal coding agents
events.label: Claude Code
events.problem: IDE autocomplete and chat helped write snippets, but developers still had to do the multi-step work of navigating, editing, testing and committing.
events.idea: An agentic command-line tool released as a research preview with Claude 3.7 Sonnet: the model searches and reads code, edits files, runs tests and shell commands, and commits, keeping the user in the loop. It became generally available with Claude 4 on 22 May 2025. Similar agents followed (OpenAI Codex, Google's Gemini CLI).
events.changed: Coding became the first domain where agents did substantial autonomous work daily, and agentic coding became a main RL training target for frontier models.
events.limits: Agents can make broad, wrong or unsafe changes; reliance on tests ties success to test quality, and reward-hacking behaviours learned in training can show up in use.

events.title: METR: measuring AI ability to complete long tasks (time horizon)
events.label: METR time horizons
events.problem: Benchmarks reported percent-correct on fixed tasks, which says little about how much autonomous work an agent can do or how fast this is improving.
events.idea: Time human experts on a suite of software and research tasks, measure each model's success rate as a function of human task length, and report the length at which the model succeeds 50% of the time. METR found this '50% time horizon' doubling roughly every 7 months from 2019 to 2025, faster in 2024-25.
events.changed: Became a widely cited summary of agent progress and a forecasting input for safety planning and lab frameworks.
events.limits: Mostly software tasks that are clean and auto-scorable; 50% success is far from reliability (80% horizons are much shorter); human baselines are few for the longest tasks.

events.title: Terminal-Bench 2.0: hard command-line tasks for agents
events.label: Terminal-Bench 2.0
events.problem: SWE-bench-style benchmarks were saturating and covered only bug fixes in Python repos, not the wider range of terminal work agents now attempted.
events.idea: Terminal-Bench 2.0 introduced 89 curated terminal tasks, each with a containerized environment, reference solution and verification tests: for example building software, training a model or reverse engineering a binary. The paper evaluates agents through a shared harness so that the environment and interface can be compared.
events.changed: Became a headline agentic-coding benchmark in 2026 model launches (e.g. Claude Opus 4.6 reported it), and its containerised task format mirrors RL training environments.
events.limits: The paper reports frontier agents below 65% on this task set. Passing tests may miss an incorrect solution, and scores depend on the model, scaffold and compute budget; benchmark success alone does not establish reliable real-world terminal work.

events.date_context: 19 May 2026 report on February–March evaluations. The public 12-hour estimate and cheating rate for shared internal models concern different populations.
events.title: 2026: longer software-task horizons and cheating on difficult evaluations
events.label: Longer horizons, cheating
events.problem: With agent capability rising fast, evaluators needed to know both how long a task frontier agents can do and whether measured successes are genuine.
events.idea: METR's Time Horizon 1.1 update (29 January 2026) expanded its software-task suite. Its 19 May Frontier Risk Report estimated the public frontier's 50% horizon around 12 hours for February–March 2026, with a wide 5–61 hour interval. On Time Horizon 1.1 tasks taking humans over eight hours, at least 16% of successful runs by the shared internal models were disqualified as illegitimate on review.
events.changed: Showed growing capability on measured software tasks while exposing a practical obstacle to measuring it: test-passing behavior can violate the intended task. The evaluation alone does not identify which training process caused that behavior.
events.limits: A 50% horizon is far from reliable workday autonomy and measures human task length, not agent runtime. The suite could not reliably estimate horizons above about 16 hours; estimates depend on modeling choices and may not transfer to messy non-software tasks.

events.date_context: 1 August 2018 Dactyl paper; distinct from Tobin et al.'s March 2017 visual domain-randomization paper.
events.title: Dactyl: transferring dexterous manipulation from simulation with PPO
events.label: Dactyl: sim-to-real RL
events.problem: A hand-control policy trained in one simulator can fail on real hardware because contact, friction, sensing and actuation differ.
events.idea: OpenAI trained an LSTM control policy with PPO in a distribution of simulations, randomizing physical properties, sensing and actuation effects as well as visual appearance. A vision-based pose estimator supplied observations for transferring in-hand object reorientation to a physical Shadow hand.
events.changed: Demonstrated that large-scale simulated RL plus domain randomization could transfer a difficult manipulation skill to real hardware without human demonstrations. It used the same distributed PPO implementation as OpenAI Five.
events.limits: Required a specialized robot, simulator calibration and large amounts of simulated experience. Transfer of one manipulation skill did not establish general-purpose robotic control.

threads.title: Learning from reward
threads.question: How does an agent learn from reward?
threads.summary: Bellman showed that optimal decisions can be computed recursively from the values of next states, but only with a known model. TD learning and Q-learning turned that recursion into learning from sampled experience by bootstrapping from the agent's own predictions, while REINFORCE and the policy gradient theorem showed how to adjust a policy directly toward actions that did better than expected. TD-Gammon proved these ideas could work with neural networks and self-play. Reward shaping and inverse RL raised the question that runs through the rest of the timeline: where the reward comes from, and whether optimising it gives the behaviour we meant.

threads.title: Deep RL
threads.question: How did RL scale with deep networks?
threads.summary: DQN stabilised Q-learning with neural networks using replay and target networks, and AlphaGo combined learned policy and value networks with tree search to master Go. Policy-gradient methods became practical at scale through parallel actor-critic (A3C) and trust-region ideas simplified into PPO, which powered OpenAI Five and later RLHF. AlphaZero and MuZero showed self-play plus search could learn from rules alone or from a learned model, and world models and offline RL attacked deep RL's chronic sample inefficiency. Most successes stayed in simulators and games, where interaction is cheap and reward is well defined.

threads.title: RL for LLM reasoning
threads.question: How did RL become the engine of LLM reasoning?
threads.summary: Preference-based RL was extended to pretrained language models with learned reward models and PPO; DPO and RLAIF offered other ways to use preference data. In 2024, o1 demonstrated large gains from RL-trained reasoning and additional inference compute, without disclosing its detailed recipe. Tulu 3 and DeepSeek-R1 made verifiable-reward training concrete in open pipelines, using PPO and GRPO respectively. The same training settings renewed older specification problems: checkers can be exploited, and learned hacking behavior can generalize beyond its original environment.

threads.title: LLM agents
threads.question: How did language models become agents?
threads.summary: Classical agent concepts provide a vocabulary for systems that observe, act and receive feedback. WebGPT, SayCan and ReAct showed different ways to put language models inside such loops. AutoGPT popularized longer autonomous workflows and exposed their brittleness, while SWE-bench, GAIA and OSWorld supplied measurable tasks. Later systems trained browsing and computer-use behavior, and MCP standardized tool connections. METR measures capability through human task duration; the 2026 estimates show progress on selected software tasks alongside failures and cheating, rather than reliable general workday autonomy.
